Starlink Constellation Simulator

⚠ Simulation, not live tracking

  • Interactive Model
  • LEO Satellite
  • Simulation

A physics-based simulation of Starlink's FCC-filed Walker-delta shells: circular Keplerian orbits with J2 drift, a day/night globe, ground tracks, coverage at a chosen minimum elevation, visibility from any place, and a simplified laser-mesh route compared with fibre. Positions come from filed shell geometry with an illustrative phasing factor, not real orbital elements.

  • 9 filed shells
  • 18,088 satellites filed across listed shells
  • Gen1: 4,408 in 5 shells (FCC 21-48)
  • Scale 10–100%, speed 1–1000×

About this model

The simulator builds each filed shell as a Walker-delta pattern and propagates circular orbits with secular J2 drift. It recomputes global coverage, average visible satellites and visibility from a chosen observer every second, and estimates propagation latency for a bent-pipe path and a laser-mesh route against great-circle fibre.

It lists what is simplified: no drag or manoeuvres, an illustrative phasing factor (F = 1), filed shell sizes rather than satellites actually in orbit, a textbook four-link +grid laser mesh within one shell, propagation delay only, and illustrative gateway markers. The start time is the moment the page is opened, so the dots are not where real Starlink satellites are.

What you can explore

  • 3D globe or ground-track map with play, speed (1× to 1000×), zoom and a 0–7 day time scrubber.
  • Minimum-elevation slider (5° to 60°), coverage heatmap, footprints, observer links, ground tracks, laser links and illustrative gateways.
  • Live stats: simulated satellites, global coverage, average visible satellites, satellites visible from the observer, the highest satellite, a latency estimate and handovers.
  • Shell toggles, a 10–100% scale, J2 precession on or off, and Gen2 at the 2026 lowered altitudes.
  • Custom shell builder (altitude, inclination, planes, satellites per plane, phasing) with period, velocity, J2 precession and footprint.
  • Laser-mesh route versus fibre between two cities, with distance, hops and latency.
